notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Mechanics explains many everyday activities involving force, motion, work, energy, pressure and machines.
  • Walking, cycling, driving, lifting, cutting, braking and turning all involve mechanical principles.
  • Simple machines make work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of force.
  • Machines do not create energy.
  • Mechanical advantage is obtained by trading force for distance or speed.
  • Friction is essential in many daily activities.
  • Pressure depends on force and area.
  • Momentum and impulse explain many safety devices.
  • Torque explains turning effects in tools and machines.
  • Newton's laws apply directly to many everyday mechanical situations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Everyday Mechanics → Force + Friction + Pressure + Torque + Work + Energy

2. Walking
  • Walking depends mainly on static friction.
  • The foot pushes the ground backward.
  • The ground exerts a forward frictional force on the foot.
  • This illustrates Newton's Third Law.
  • Without sufficient friction, walking becomes difficult.
  • Wet or icy surfaces reduce friction and increase slipping risk.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Walking → Static Friction + Newton III

3. Running
  • Running requires greater force against the ground than slow walking.
  • Athletes push the ground backward.
  • The ground provides a forward reaction force.
  • Spiked shoes increase friction with the track.
  • Greater grip allows a runner to accelerate more effectively.
4. Standing
  • A person standing still is in mechanical equilibrium.
  • Body weight acts downward.
  • The ground provides an upward normal reaction.
  • If these forces balance, vertical acceleration is zero.
  • Stability increases when the centre of gravity lies within the base of support.
5. Bending the Body
  • Bending changes the position of the body's centre of gravity.
  • A person may spread the feet to increase the base of support.
  • A wider base improves stability.
  • Keeping the centre of gravity low improves stability.
  • Wrestlers and athletes often lower their body position to become more stable.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stability → Wide Base + Low Centre of Gravity

6. Carrying a Load
  • Carrying a load increases the total weight supported by the body.
  • A load held far from the body produces greater torque about the spine.
  • Holding a load close to the body reduces the moment arm.
  • Therefore, carrying a heavy object close to the body reduces mechanical strain.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Load closer to body → Smaller torque

7. Lifting a Load
  • When lifting, muscles apply force against gravity.
  • Mechanical work is done when the load is displaced upward.
  • Work against gravity is approximately mgh.
  • Bending the knees and keeping the load close reduces torque on the lower back.
  • A sudden lift can create larger forces than a slow controlled lift.
8. Human Body as a Lever System
  • Bones act as levers.
  • Joints act as fulcrums.
  • Muscles provide effort.
  • Body weight or external load provides resistance.
  • Many human limb movements involve third-class levers.
  • Third-class levers provide speed and range of motion rather than force multiplication.
9. Human Forearm
  • The elbow acts as the fulcrum.
  • Biceps provide effort.
  • The load is usually in the hand.
  • Effort lies between fulcrum and load.
  • Therefore, the forearm with biceps is a third-class lever.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Human Forearm → Third-Class Lever

10. Head on Neck
  • The joint between skull and vertebral column acts as fulcrum.
  • Weight of head acts on one side.
  • Neck muscles exert effort on the other side.
  • This is commonly treated as a first-class lever.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Head on Neck → First-Class Lever

11. Standing on Toes
  • The toes act as the fulcrum.
  • Body weight acts as load.
  • Calf muscles provide effort through the Achilles tendon.
  • The load lies between fulcrum and effort.
  • Standing on toes is a second-class lever.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Standing on Toes → Second-Class Lever

12. Scissors
  • Scissors are first-class levers.
  • The pivot screw is the fulcrum.
  • Effort is applied at the handles.
  • Load acts at the cutting blades.
  • Fulcrum lies between effort and load.
  • Scissors also use wedge-like cutting edges.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Scissors → First-Class Lever + Wedge

13. Pliers
  • Pliers are first-class levers.
  • Pivot is between effort and load.
  • Longer handles increase mechanical advantage.
  • Pliers multiply gripping force.
14. Crowbar
  • A crowbar often works as a first-class lever.
  • The fulcrum lies between effort and load.
  • Increasing effort-arm length reduces the required effort.
  • Crowbars are used to lift or pry heavy objects.
15. Seesaw
  • A seesaw is a first-class lever.
  • Fulcrum lies at the centre.
  • Balance depends on moments on both sides.
  • Heavier child can balance lighter child by sitting closer to the fulcrum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Balance → Weight × Distance from Fulcrum

16. Wheelbarrow
  • A wheelbarrow is a second-class lever.
  • Wheel axle acts as fulcrum.
  • Load lies between fulcrum and effort.
  • Effort is applied at the handles.
  • Second-class levers generally provide mechanical advantage greater than one.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wheelbarrow → Second-Class Lever

17. Nutcracker
  • A nutcracker is a second-class lever.
  • Hinge is the fulcrum.
  • Nut is the load.
  • Effort is applied at handles.
  • Load lies between fulcrum and effort.
18. Bottle Opener
  • A bottle opener commonly acts as a second-class lever.
  • Bottle rim provides fulcrum.
  • Cap is the load.
  • Effort is applied at the handle.
  • Mechanical advantage helps remove the cap.
19. Tweezers
  • Tweezers are third-class levers.
  • One joined end acts as fulcrum.
  • Effort is applied between fulcrum and load.
  • Load acts at tips.
  • Third-class levers favour speed and precision of movement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tweezers → Third-Class Lever

20. Fishing Rod
  • A fishing rod commonly functions as a third-class lever.
  • One hand may act as fulcrum.
  • The other hand provides effort.
  • Fish acts as load at the far end.
  • It provides large movement at the rod tip.
21. Broom
  • A broom can function as a third-class lever.
  • One hand acts approximately as fulcrum.
  • Other hand provides effort.
  • Broom head acts as load.
  • Effort lies between fulcrum and load.
22. Lever Classes — Must Remember
  • First class → Fulcrum in middle.
  • Second class → Load in middle.
  • Third class → Effort in middle.
📌 Memory

FLE

First → Fulcrum

Second → Load

Third → Effort

23. Knife
  • A knife functions as a wedge.
  • A wedge converts downward force into forces acting sideways.
  • A sharp knife has a smaller contact area.
  • Smaller area produces greater pressure for the same force.
  • Therefore, sharp knives cut more easily.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sharp Knife → Small Area → High Pressure

24. Needle
  • A needle has a very small pointed area.
  • The applied force acts over a tiny area.
  • This produces high pressure.
  • High pressure allows the needle to penetrate material.
25. Nail
  • A nail has a pointed tip to create high pressure.
  • Hammering applies a large force.
  • Small tip area concentrates this force.
  • Friction between nail and material helps hold it in place.
26. Axe
  • An axe head acts as a wedge.
  • The wedge converts force into sideways splitting forces.
  • A sharp axe concentrates force over a smaller area.
  • Greater pressure assists cutting.
27. Screw
  • A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder.
  • Rotation produces linear motion.
  • Fine threads increase mechanical advantage.
  • Screws are used to fasten objects tightly.
  • Screw jacks use the same principle to lift heavy loads.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Screw → Inclined Plane Wrapped Around Cylinder

28. Screw Jack
  • A screw jack converts rotational effort into large upward force.
  • A long handle increases torque.
  • Small thread pitch gives greater mechanical advantage.
  • More rotations are required for a small vertical rise.
  • It trades distance for force.
29. Door Handle
  • Door handles are placed far from hinges.
  • Torque = Force × perpendicular distance.
  • Greater distance from hinge produces greater torque.
  • Therefore, less force is required to open the door.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Door Handle Far from Hinge → Larger Torque

30. Spanner / Wrench
  • A spanner applies torque to a nut or bolt.
  • A longer spanner produces greater torque for the same force.
  • Applying force perpendicular to the spanner maximises torque.
  • Torque is τ = rF sinθ.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Longer Spanner → Greater Turning Effect

31. Steering Wheel
  • A steering wheel is an example of wheel and axle.
  • Large radius helps produce greater torque.
  • Turning the wheel rotates the steering shaft.
  • Steering systems may also use power assistance.
32. Wheel and Axle
  • Wheel and axle is a simple machine.
  • A large wheel is fixed to a smaller axle.
  • It can multiply torque.
  • Door knobs and steering wheels use this principle.
  • Mechanical advantage depends on ratio of radii.
33. Pulley
  • A pulley consists of a grooved wheel and rope.
  • Pulley systems can change force direction.
  • They can also provide mechanical advantage.
  • Pulleys are used in wells, cranes and elevators.
34. Fixed Pulley
  • A fixed pulley remains attached to a support.
  • It mainly changes direction of effort.
  • Ideal mechanical advantage is 1.
  • Pulling downward can raise a load upward.
  • It does not ideally reduce the magnitude of force required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fixed Pulley → Direction Change

35. Movable Pulley
  • A movable pulley moves with the load.
  • It provides mechanical advantage.
  • In an ideal single movable pulley, mechanical advantage can be 2.
  • Effort required is approximately half the load, ignoring friction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Movable Pulley → Force Multiplication

36. Block and Tackle
  • Block and tackle combines fixed and movable pulleys.
  • More supporting rope segments increase ideal mechanical advantage.
  • It is used to lift heavy loads.
  • Cranes and workshops use pulley systems.
37. Well Pulley
  • A pulley at a well changes the direction of applied force.
  • Pulling the rope downward raises the bucket.
  • A fixed pulley mainly provides convenience rather than force multiplication.
38. Crane
  • Cranes use pulleys, cables and levers.
  • Counterweights improve stability.
  • Cranes must keep the combined centre of gravity within the support base.
  • Long booms create large torque.
  • Load limits prevent overturning.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Crane Stability → Counterweight + Torque Balance

39. Inclined Plane
  • An inclined plane reduces required force by increasing movement distance.
  • Ramps are inclined planes.
  • Loading ramps make it easier to move heavy objects to greater height.
  • Ideal work remains the same even though force is reduced.
40. Staircase
  • A staircase functions like a series of inclined planes.
  • It allows elevation to be gained gradually.
  • Smaller vertical rise per step reduces force and effort difficulty compared with climbing vertically.
41. Ramp
  • A ramp reduces the force required to raise an object.
  • Longer gentle ramps require less force but greater travel distance.
  • Wheelchair ramps use this mechanical principle.
42. Bicycle — Basic Mechanics
  • A bicycle uses wheels, axles, levers, gears and friction.
  • Pedalling provides torque.
  • Chain transfers rotational motion from front chainring to rear sprocket.
  • Tyre-road friction enables forward motion.
  • Brakes use friction to reduce speed.
43. Bicycle Gears
  • Gears change torque and rotational speed.
  • A lower gear provides greater mechanical advantage for climbing.
  • A higher gear allows greater distance per pedal revolution on level roads.
  • Gear choice trades force against speed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Low Gear → Easier Climbing + More Torque

High Gear → Greater Speed per Pedal Revolution

44. Gear
  • A gear is a toothed wheel.
  • Meshing gears transfer rotational motion and torque.
  • Adjacent meshing gears rotate in opposite directions.
  • A small driving gear turning a large driven gear reduces speed and increases torque.
  • A large driving gear turning a small driven gear increases speed and reduces torque.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Small driver → Large driven → Speed ↓, Torque ↑

Large driver → Small driven → Speed ↑, Torque ↓

45. Bicycle Brakes
  • Bicycle brakes use friction.
  • Brake pads press against wheel rim or brake disc.
  • Friction converts kinetic energy into heat.
  • Greater braking force produces greater deceleration up to the limit of tyre-road grip.
  • Excessive braking can cause skidding or wheel lock.
46. Motor Vehicle Motion
  • Engine or motor provides driving force.
  • Tyres push backward on road.
  • Road exerts forward frictional force on tyres.
  • Air drag and rolling resistance oppose motion.
  • At constant velocity, driving force balances resistive forces.
  • During acceleration, driving force is greater than resistive forces.
47. Vehicle Brakes
  • Brakes convert kinetic energy mainly into heat through friction.
  • Disc brakes use friction between pads and rotating disc.
  • Drum brakes use friction between brake shoes and drum.
  • Braking distance increases strongly with vehicle speed.
  • Kinetic energy varies as v².
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Speed × 2 → KE × 4 → More Energy to Remove During Braking

48. Hydraulic Brakes
  • Hydraulic brakes operate using Pascal's principle.
  • Pressure applied to brake fluid is transmitted through the fluid.
  • A small input force can produce larger force at brake pistons.
  • Brake fluid must be nearly incompressible.
  • Hydraulic systems provide smooth force transmission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hydraulic Brake → Pascal's Law

49. Seat Belt
  • Seat belts protect against inertia during sudden stopping.
  • A passenger tends to continue moving forward when the vehicle stops.
  • Seat belts provide the force needed to decelerate the passenger.
  • They increase stopping time.
  • Longer stopping time reduces average force for the same momentum change.
  • They also distribute force across stronger body regions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Seat Belt → Inertia + Impulse

50. Airbag
  • Airbags increase the time over which momentum changes.
  • Greater stopping time reduces average force.
  • Airbags increase the area over which force acts.
  • Larger contact area reduces pressure on the body.
  • Airbags work together with seat belts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Airbag → Time ↑ + Area ↑ → Injury Force/Pressure ↓

51. Crumple Zone
  • Crumple zones are designed to deform during collision.
  • Deformation increases collision time.
  • It absorbs part of vehicle kinetic energy.
  • Greater collision time reduces peak force on occupants.
  • Passenger compartment is designed to remain more rigid.
52. Headrest
  • A headrest reduces backward movement of the head relative to the torso during certain rear impacts.
  • It reduces risk of whiplash injury.
  • Proper headrest position is important for effectiveness.
53. Helmet
  • A helmet increases impact time by deformation of cushioning material.
  • It absorbs and redistributes impact energy.
  • It spreads force over a larger area.
  • Larger area reduces pressure on the skull.
  • Helmets reduce head-injury risk.
54. Vehicle Tyres
  • Tyres provide friction with road.
  • Treads help maintain grip, particularly by channeling water.
  • Worn tyres reduce grip.
  • Proper tyre pressure affects contact, rolling resistance and vehicle control.
55. Wide Tyres
  • Wide tyres can help distribute load over larger ground area.
  • Tractors use wide tyres to reduce pressure on soft soil.
  • Heavy vehicles may use multiple tyres to distribute load.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Area ↑ → Pressure ↓

56. Tractor Tyres
  • Tractor tyres are broad.
  • Broad tyres reduce pressure on agricultural soil.
  • Deep treads increase grip.
  • Large rear wheels also improve traction on soft surfaces.
57. Tank Tracks
  • Tanks use broad continuous tracks.
  • Tracks spread weight over a large area.
  • This reduces ground pressure.
  • Tracks also improve traction on soft or uneven terrain.
58. Snow Shoes
  • Snow shoes have a large surface area.
  • They distribute body weight over a larger area.
  • Pressure on snow is reduced.
  • This prevents deep sinking.
59. High Heels
  • High heels have small contact area.
  • For the same body weight, smaller area creates greater pressure on the ground.
  • This is why high heels can sink more deeply into soft surfaces than flat shoes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

High Heel → Small Area → High Pressure

60. School Bag Strap
  • Wide shoulder straps distribute force over a larger area.
  • Larger area reduces pressure on shoulders.
  • Narrow straps produce greater pressure for the same load.
61. Sharp Needle vs Blunt Needle
  • A sharp needle has smaller tip area.
  • Same force produces greater pressure.
  • A blunt needle requires greater force for penetration.
62. Dam Wall
  • Liquid pressure increases with depth.
  • Therefore, dam walls are made thicker at the bottom.
  • Greater depth means greater water pressure.
  • Hydrostatic pressure is P = ρgh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dam Bottom → Thicker because Pressure ↑ with Depth

63. Water Tank
  • Water pressure is greater at lower outlets.
  • A hole near the bottom of a tank produces faster outflow than an equal hole near the top.
  • Greater liquid head produces greater pressure.
  • Torricelli's relation explains efflux speed approximately as v = √(2gh).
64. Water Supply Towers
  • Elevated water tanks provide gravitational potential energy.
  • Height creates hydrostatic pressure.
  • Greater height can provide greater pressure at lower delivery points.
  • Water can flow without continuous pumping when sufficient head exists.
65. Hydraulic Lift
  • Hydraulic lifts work on Pascal's principle.
  • A small force acts on a small piston.
  • Pressure is transmitted through fluid.
  • A larger piston produces a larger output force.
  • Vehicle service stations use hydraulic lifts.
📌 Formula

F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂

66. Hydraulic Press
  • Hydraulic press multiplies force using different piston areas.
  • It works on Pascal's law.
  • It is used in compressing, shaping and lifting materials.
  • Large force can be generated from smaller input effort.
67. Syringe
  • A syringe uses pressure difference to draw and expel liquid.
  • Pulling the plunger increases internal volume and lowers pressure.
  • External atmospheric pressure helps push liquid into the syringe.
  • Pushing the plunger increases pressure and expels liquid.
68. Drinking Straw
  • Sucking reduces air pressure inside the straw.
  • Atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface pushes liquid upward.
  • Liquid is not literally “pulled” upward by suction alone.
  • The maximum height is limited by atmospheric pressure and liquid density.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Straw → Atmospheric pressure pushes liquid upward.

69. Dropper
  • A dropper works using pressure differences.
  • Squeezing the rubber bulb expels air.
  • Releasing it reduces internal pressure.
  • Atmospheric pressure pushes liquid into the dropper.
70. Suction Cup
  • Pressing a suction cup removes much of the air beneath it.
  • Lower pressure remains inside.
  • Greater atmospheric pressure outside holds the cup against the surface.
  • It does not work well if air leaks underneath.
71. Vacuum Cleaner
  • A vacuum cleaner creates lower air pressure inside its intake.
  • Higher surrounding atmospheric pressure pushes air and dust toward the intake.
  • A fan creates the pressure difference.
  • Filters trap dust particles.
72. Atomiser / Perfume Sprayer
  • Fast-moving air can lower static pressure in a narrow region.
  • Liquid rises due to pressure difference.
  • Airflow breaks liquid into droplets.
  • Bernoulli-related effects are involved.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Atomiser → Fast Air + Low Pressure

73. Carburettor — Classical Principle
  • Traditional carburettors use pressure differences caused by fast airflow.
  • A Venturi section increases air speed.
  • Reduced pressure draws fuel into the airstream.
  • Modern vehicles commonly use electronic fuel injection instead.
74. Venturimeter
  • A Venturimeter measures fluid flow rate.
  • It uses a narrowing in a pipe.
  • Fluid speed increases in narrow region.
  • Static pressure decreases.
  • It uses Bernoulli's principle and continuity equation.
75. Airplane Wing
  • Aircraft wings generate lift by changing airflow momentum and producing pressure differences.
  • Wing shape and angle of attack influence lift.
  • Faster airflow can be associated with lower static pressure under Bernoulli conditions.
  • Newton's laws also explain lift through downward deflection of air.
  • Lift must balance or exceed weight for level flight or climb.
76. Aeroplane Take-Off
  • Engine provides thrust.
  • Air resistance provides drag.
  • Wings provide lift.
  • Gravity provides weight.
  • During take-off, sufficient lift must be generated.
  • Increasing airspeed generally increases lift up to operating limits.
📌 Must-Memorise Aircraft Forces

Lift → Up

Weight → Down

Thrust → Forward

Drag → Backward

77. Parachute
  • A parachute increases air resistance.
  • Greater drag reduces acceleration.
  • Eventually a lower terminal velocity is reached.
  • Lower landing speed reduces kinetic energy and impact force.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Parachute → Drag ↑ → Terminal Velocity ↓

78. Streamlining
  • Streamlining reduces fluid drag.
  • Cars, aircraft, ships and fish have streamlined shapes.
  • Reduced drag improves efficiency and speed.
  • Streamlining reduces turbulence and pressure resistance in suitable conditions.
79. Boats and Ships
  • Ships float because of buoyant force.
  • Archimedes' principle applies.
  • A floating ship displaces water equal in weight to the ship.
  • Hollow ship construction lowers average density.
  • Greater load makes a ship sink deeper until more water is displaced.
80. Submarine
  • Submarines adjust buoyancy with ballast tanks.
  • Filling tanks with water increases average density.
  • Blowing water out with compressed air decreases average density.
  • Neutral buoyancy permits approximately constant depth.
81. Life Jacket
  • A life jacket contains low-density material or air.
  • It increases the person's total volume without greatly increasing mass.
  • Average density of the person-jacket system decreases.
  • Buoyant force increases.
  • This helps keep the wearer afloat.
82. Swimming
  • Swimmers push water backward.
  • Water exerts a forward reaction force.
  • Buoyancy supports part of body weight.
  • Streamlined body position reduces drag.
  • Swimming illustrates Newton's Third Law and fluid mechanics.
83. Rowing a Boat
  • Oars push water backward.
  • Water exerts a forward force on the boat.
  • This illustrates Newton's Third Law.
  • The oar itself also functions as a lever.
84. Rocket
  • Rockets expel gases backward at high velocity.
  • Rocket gains forward momentum.
  • Rocket propulsion follows conservation of momentum.
  • It also illustrates Newton's Third Law.
  • Rockets work in vacuum.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rocket does not push against air.

85. Gun Recoil
  • Bullet moves forward.
  • Gun recoils backward.
  • Total momentum is conserved.
  • Gun's larger mass results in smaller recoil velocity.
  • This also illustrates Newton's Third Law.
86. Cricket Catch
  • A cricketer moves hands backward while catching.
  • This increases stopping time.
  • For the same change in momentum, greater time reduces average force.
  • This is an application of impulse.
87. Cricket Bat Follow-Through
  • Follow-through increases time over which the bat interacts with the ball.
  • It can help produce a larger impulse.
  • Larger impulse produces a greater change in ball momentum.
88. Long Jump Sand Pit
  • Sand increases stopping time and stopping distance.
  • Greater stopping time reduces average impact force.
  • Sand also deforms and absorbs energy.
  • This reduces injury risk.
89. High Jump Mat
  • Soft landing mats deform.
  • Deformation increases stopping time.
  • Average impact force is reduced.
  • The mat also spreads force over a wider area.
90. Boxing Gloves
  • Boxing gloves provide padding.
  • Padding increases impact duration.
  • Greater contact time reduces peak force.
  • Larger contact area reduces pressure.
  • Gloves do not eliminate momentum transfer.
91. Hammer
  • A hammer's heavy head has significant momentum when swung.
  • Higher speed greatly increases kinetic energy.
  • Impact transfers momentum and energy to the nail.
  • Long handle allows greater swing speed and torque.
92. Axe and Hammer Handles
  • Long handles increase leverage and tip speed.
  • Greater radius can produce higher linear speed for the same angular speed.
  • This increases kinetic energy before impact.
  • Proper grip improves control.
93. Balancing a Bicycle
  • A moving bicycle is easier to stabilise because steering corrections can continually place the wheels beneath the centre of mass.
  • Rotating wheels contribute some gyroscopic effects.
  • Bicycle stability is not due to gyroscopic effect alone.
  • Steering geometry and rider control are also important.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bicycle balance is not explained solely by gyroscopic effect.

94. Road Banking
  • Curved roads are banked to assist turning.
  • A component of normal reaction provides centripetal force.
  • Banking reduces dependence on friction.
  • It is especially useful for high-speed curves.
95. Road Friction
  • Tyre-road friction provides force needed for acceleration, braking and turning.
  • Wet roads may reduce available friction.
  • Oil or ice greatly reduces grip.
  • Tyre tread helps maintain contact by removing water.
96. Skidding
  • Skidding occurs when required friction exceeds available static friction.
  • Once sliding begins, kinetic friction may be lower than maximum static friction.
  • Excessive speed on a curve increases required centripetal force.
  • Wet roads increase skidding risk.
97. Anti-Lock Braking System
  • ABS stands for Anti-lock Braking System.
  • ABS helps prevent wheels from locking during hard braking.
  • It allows tyres to retain better steering control.
  • It attempts to keep tyre-road interaction near useful high-friction conditions.
  • ABS does not eliminate the laws of friction or guarantee short stopping distance on every surface.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ABS → Prevent Wheel Lock + Maintain Steering Control

98. Speed and Braking Distance
  • Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared.
  • Doubling vehicle speed gives four times the kinetic energy.
  • More energy must be removed by brakes.
  • Therefore, braking distance generally increases strongly with speed.
  • Reaction distance also increases with speed.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Speed doubling does not merely double kinetic energy.

It quadruples it.

99. Lift / Elevator
  • A lift accelerating upward has greater apparent weight.
  • A lift accelerating downward has lower apparent weight.
  • At constant velocity, apparent weight equals normal weight.
  • In free fall, apparent weight becomes zero.
  • A weighing scale measures normal reaction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lift Up Accelerating → Apparent Weight ↑

Lift Down Accelerating → Apparent Weight ↓

Free Fall → Apparent Weight 0

100. Apparent Weight in Lift
  • Upward acceleration: N = m(g + a).
  • Downward acceleration: N = m(g − a).
  • Constant velocity: N = mg.
  • Free fall: a = g downward, so N = 0.
101. Escalator
  • An escalator continuously moves steps using a motor.
  • Motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
  • A person standing on a moving escalator gains gravitational potential energy as height increases.
  • Power depends on rate of energy transfer.
102. Conveyor Belt
  • Conveyor belts move objects using friction.
  • Static friction can accelerate an object placed on a moving belt until it moves with the belt.
  • Motors provide mechanical energy.
  • Friction between belt and object prevents slipping under suitable conditions.
103. Ball Bearings
  • Ball bearings reduce friction.
  • They replace much sliding friction with rolling friction.
  • They are used in wheels, motors and machines.
  • Reduced friction lowers heating and energy loss.
104. Lubrication
  • Lubricants reduce friction between moving surfaces.
  • Oil forms a thin layer between surfaces.
  • Reduced friction decreases wear.
  • It also reduces heat production and energy loss.
  • Lubrication improves machine efficiency.
105. Flywheel
  • A flywheel is a rotating mechanical energy-storage device.
  • It stores rotational kinetic energy.
  • It helps smooth variations in rotational speed.
  • Flywheels are used in engines and machinery.
  • Greater moment of inertia allows more rotational energy storage at a given angular speed.
106. Ceiling Fan
  • Electric motor converts electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy.
  • Rotating blades push air.
  • Airflow produces cooling mainly by increasing evaporation and convective heat transfer from the body.
  • A fan does not significantly lower room air temperature in a closed room; its motor adds some heat.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Fan mainly cools people, not the room itself.

107. Mixer / Grinder
  • Electric motor converts electrical energy into rotational energy.
  • Blades rotate at high speed.
  • Rotating blades apply force and shear to food material.
  • Friction can also produce heat.
108. Washing Machine Spin Cycle
  • Drum rotates rapidly.
  • Water tends to move outward relative to the rotating drum because of inertia.
  • Holes allow water to leave.
  • In the rotating frame, this is often described using centrifugal effect.
  • Clothes remain within the drum.
109. Centrifuge
  • A centrifuge spins mixtures at high speed.
  • Components separate according to differences in density and sedimentation behaviour.
  • Denser components move outward more strongly in the rotating frame.
  • Centrifuges are used in laboratories and medicine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Centrifuge → Separation by Rapid Rotation

110. Spin Dryer
  • Spin dryers use rapid rotation.
  • Water is expelled through holes in rotating drum.
  • Inertia of water contributes to separation.
  • This is commonly described as centrifugal action in the rotating frame.
111. Banked Railway Track
  • Outer rail is raised at curves.
  • Banking helps provide required centripetal force.
  • It reduces lateral stress on rails and wheels.
  • Appropriate banking improves safety.
112. Railway Track Gaps
  • Metals expand when heated.
  • Railway tracks require allowance for thermal expansion.
  • Expansion joints or suitable rail engineering prevents buckling.
  • Bridges also require expansion provisions.
113. Expansion Joint in Bridges
  • Bridges expand in hot weather and contract in cold weather.
  • Expansion joints allow this movement.
  • Without provision, thermal stress could damage structures.
114. Dam and Retaining Structures
  • Fluid pressure increases with depth.
  • Lower portions must withstand greater pressure.
  • This is why dam walls are generally thicker at the bottom.
115. Mechanical Advantage
  • Mechanical advantage = Load/Effort.
  • MA greater than 1 indicates force multiplication.
  • MA has no unit.
  • A machine may provide force, speed or directional advantage.
116. Velocity Ratio
  • Velocity ratio = Distance moved by effort / Distance moved by load.
  • It depends mainly on machine geometry.
  • It has no unit.
  • For an ideal machine, MA = VR.
117. Efficiency of Machine
  • Efficiency = Useful output work / Input work × 100%.
  • Efficiency = MA/VR × 100% for a simple machine.
  • Real machines have efficiency below 100%.
  • Friction reduces efficiency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Real Machine → Efficiency < 100%

118. Why Machines Cannot Save Work Ideally
  • A machine may reduce force required.
  • But the effort generally moves through a greater distance.
  • Ideal work input equals work output.
  • Machines provide convenience rather than free energy.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Machine saves force, not energy.

119. Everyday Pressure Applications
  • Sharp knife → High pressure.
  • Needle → High pressure.
  • Nail → High pressure.
  • Broad tyre → Low pressure.
  • Snowshoe → Low pressure.
  • Wide bag strap → Low pressure.
  • Dam bottom → High liquid pressure.
  • Hydraulic lift → Pascal's principle.
120. Everyday Friction Applications
  • Walking → Static friction.
  • Brakes → Friction.
  • Tyres → Road friction.
  • Writing → Friction.
  • Matchstick → Frictional heating.
  • Ball bearing → Reduces friction.
  • Lubricant → Reduces friction.
  • Spikes → Increase friction.
121. Everyday Newton's Law Applications
  • Bus suddenly starts → Inertia of rest.
  • Bus suddenly stops → Inertia of motion.
  • Turning vehicle → Inertia of direction.
  • Walking → Newton III.
  • Swimming → Newton III.
  • Rocket → Newton III.
  • Gun recoil → Newton III.
  • F = ma → Newton II.
  • Seat belt → Newton I + Impulse.
122. Everyday Torque Applications
  • Door handle far from hinge.
  • Long spanner.
  • Steering wheel.
  • Screwdriver.
  • Pedal crank.
  • Crowbar.
  • Seesaw.
  • Wheelbarrow.
  • Screw jack.
123. Everyday Momentum and Impulse Applications
  • Seat belt.
  • Airbag.
  • Crumple zone.
  • Cricket catch.
  • High-jump mat.
  • Boxing glove.
  • Helmet.
  • Gun recoil.
  • Rocket propulsion.
124. Must-Memorise Simple Machines
  • Lever.
  • Wheel and axle.
  • Pulley.
  • Inclined plane.
  • Wedge.
  • Screw.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

All simple machines → Trade force against distance/direction

125. Important Formulae
  • Pressure → P = F/A.
  • Work → W = Fs cosθ.
  • Power → P = W/t.
  • Torque → τ = rF sinθ.
  • Momentum → p = mv.
  • Impulse → FΔt = Δp.
  • Kinetic energy → ½mv².
  • Potential energy → mgh.
  • Mechanical advantage → Load/Effort.
  • Efficiency → Output/Input × 100%.
  • Hydraulic system → F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
  • Hydrostatic pressure → P = ρgh.
126. TNPSC Traps
  • Walking depends on static friction, not sliding friction.
  • A fixed pulley mainly changes force direction.
  • A movable pulley provides force advantage.
  • Machines do not create energy.
  • A sharp knife works because smaller area produces greater pressure.
  • Wide straps reduce pressure.
  • Dam walls are thicker at the bottom because liquid pressure increases with depth.
  • Hydraulic brakes work on Pascal's principle.
  • A straw works because atmospheric pressure pushes liquid upward.
  • A suction cup is held by atmospheric pressure difference.
  • Seat belts work through inertia and impulse.
  • Airbags increase collision time and contact area.
  • Crumple zones are designed to deform.
  • Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.
  • Rocket propulsion does not require air.
  • A ship floats because of buoyancy, not because metal itself is lighter than water.
  • Life jackets increase volume and buoyancy.
  • Road banking reduces dependence on friction.
  • Geometrical gear size determines speed-torque trade-off.
  • ABS helps prevent wheel lock but does not eliminate stopping distance.
  • In a lift moving at constant velocity, apparent weight equals normal weight.
  • In free fall, apparent weight is zero.
  • A ceiling fan mainly increases heat loss from the body rather than lowering room temperature.
  • Ball bearings reduce friction by replacing sliding with rolling.
  • A centrifuge separates materials through rotational motion and density-dependent sedimentation.
127. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Walking → Friction.
  • Forearm → Third lever.
  • Toes → Second lever.
  • Scissors → First lever.
  • Knife → Wedge.
  • Screw → Inclined plane wrapped.
  • Door → Torque.
  • Spanner → Longer = easier.
  • Fixed pulley → Direction.
  • Movable pulley → Force advantage.
  • Bicycle gear → Torque-speed trade.
  • Brake → Friction.
  • Hydraulic brake → Pascal.
  • Seat belt → Inertia + impulse.
  • Airbag → Time ↑, force ↓.
  • Dam → Pressure ↑ with depth.
  • Straw → Atmospheric pressure.
  • Plane → Lift + thrust.
  • Parachute → Drag.
  • Ship → Buoyancy.
  • Submarine → Ballast.
  • Rocket → Newton III.
  • Cricket catch → Impulse.
  • Lift up → Weight ↑.
  • Lift down → Weight ↓.
  • Free fall → Weightlessness.
  • Ball bearing → Rolling friction.
  • Lubricant → Friction ↓.
  • Centrifuge → Rotation.
  • Machine → Cannot create energy.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Walking mainly depends on? → Static friction.
  • Walking illustrates which Newton law? → Newton's Third Law.
  • Best condition for stability? → Low centre of gravity and wide base.
  • Why carry a heavy load close to body? → To reduce torque on the spine.
  • Bones act as? → Levers.
  • Joints act as? → Fulcrums.
  • Muscles provide? → Effort.
  • Human forearm with biceps? → Third-class lever.
  • Standing on toes? → Second-class lever.
  • Head balanced on neck? → First-class lever.
  • Scissors? → First-class lever.
  • Wheelbarrow? → Second-class lever.
  • Nutcracker? → Second-class lever.
  • Tweezers? → Third-class lever.
  • First-class lever has what in middle? → Fulcrum.
  • Second-class lever has what in middle? → Load.
  • Third-class lever has what in middle? → Effort.
  • Why does a sharp knife cut easily? → Smaller area produces greater pressure.
  • A screw is essentially? → Inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder.
  • Why is door handle far from hinge? → To increase torque.
  • Why is a long spanner easier to use? → Greater moment arm gives greater torque.
  • Fixed pulley mainly does what? → Changes direction of force.
  • Ideal MA of single fixed pulley? → 1.
  • Movable pulley provides? → Mechanical advantage.
  • Block and tackle consists of? → Fixed and movable pulleys.
  • Ramp is an example of? → Inclined plane.
  • Low bicycle gear provides? → More torque / easier climbing.
  • High bicycle gear provides? → Greater speed per pedal revolution.
  • Small driving gear with large driven gear gives? → Lower speed, higher torque.
  • Vehicle brakes convert kinetic energy mainly into? → Heat.
  • Hydraulic brakes work on? → Pascal's principle.
  • Seat belt protects mainly against? → Inertia during sudden stopping.
  • Why does seat belt reduce force? → It increases stopping time.
  • Airbag reduces injury by? → Increasing stopping time and contact area.
  • Crumple zone purpose? → Increase collision time and absorb energy.
  • Why are tractor tyres broad? → To reduce ground pressure.
  • Why do high heels exert more pressure? → Small contact area.
  • Why are school-bag straps wide? → To reduce pressure.
  • Why is dam wall thicker at bottom? → Water pressure increases with depth.
  • Hydrostatic pressure formula? → ρgh.
  • Hydraulic-lift relation? → F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
  • What pushes water up a straw? → Atmospheric pressure.
  • Suction cup is held by? → Atmospheric-pressure difference.
  • Vacuum cleaner works mainly through? → Pressure difference.
  • Atomiser works with? → Fast airflow and pressure reduction.
  • Four forces on an aircraft? → Lift, weight, thrust and drag.
  • Parachute reduces speed by increasing? → Drag.
  • Streamlining reduces? → Fluid resistance.
  • Why does a ship float? → Buoyant force balances its weight.
  • Floating body displaces fluid equal in weight to? → Its own weight.
  • Submarine controls depth using? → Ballast tanks.
  • Life jacket increases? → Buoyancy by reducing average density.
  • Swimming illustrates? → Newton's Third Law.
  • Rocket propulsion based on? → Newton's Third Law and conservation of momentum.
  • Can rocket move in vacuum? → Yes.
  • Gun recoil based on? → Conservation of momentum.
  • Why does cricketer move hands backward while catching? → To increase stopping time and reduce force.
  • Why is sand pit used in long jump? → Increases stopping time and reduces impact force.
  • Why are boxing gloves padded? → Increase impact time and spread force.
  • Road banking helps provide? → Centripetal force.
  • Why do vehicles skid? → Required friction exceeds available friction.
  • ABS stands for? → Anti-lock Braking System.
  • Purpose of ABS? → Prevent wheel lock and preserve steering control.
  • If vehicle speed doubles, kinetic energy becomes? → Four times.
  • Lift accelerating upward causes apparent weight to? → Increase.
  • Lift accelerating downward causes apparent weight to? → Decrease.
  • Lift moving at constant velocity gives apparent weight? → mg.
  • Apparent weight in free fall? → Zero.
  • Upward lift formula? → N = m(g + a).
  • Downward lift formula? → N = m(g − a).
  • Ball bearings reduce? → Friction.
  • How do ball bearings reduce friction? → Replace sliding friction with rolling friction.
  • Lubricants reduce? → Friction and wear.
  • A flywheel stores? → Rotational kinetic energy.
  • Ceiling fan mainly cools a person by? → Increasing evaporation and convection.
  • Spin dryer works using? → Rapid rotation and centrifugal effect in the rotating frame.
  • Centrifuge is used for? → Separating components through rapid rotation.
  • Why are gaps/expansion provisions needed in bridges and tracks? → Thermal expansion.
  • Mechanical advantage formula? → Load/Effort.
  • Efficiency formula? → Useful output/Input × 100%.
  • Can a real machine be 100% efficient? → No.
  • Do machines create energy? → No.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Knife → Pressure; Door handle → Torque; Brake → Friction; Hydraulic brake → Pascal; Seat belt → Impulse; Ship → Archimedes; Road banking → Centripetal force; Rocket → Newton III.
